newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Folgado sees further progress in 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Folgado sees further progress in 1997 budget.

text.p: Spain will outperform some of its budgetary forecasts for 1997, but financial markets may fail to take immediate advantage having already raced higher in recent months, Spanish Budget Secretary Jose Folgado said on Monday.

Spain will reach its target for three percent deficit to gross domestic product for 1997, down from 4.4 percent in 1996. It will also surpass its initial target for debt reduction, Folgado told Reuters in an interview.
"I'm totally convinced of making it," Folgado said, referring to the deficit target.
Debt to GDP would outperform the goal of 67.2 percent for 1997, down from 67.5 percent in 1996.
"It (debt) is going to be clearly better than in the budget," Folgado said.

Spain budgeted for receipts of 450 billion pesetas ($3.3 billion) from privatisations, all of which will be used to retire debt. In addition, savings in interest rate payments as official rates declined would also be devoted to retiring debt, Folgado added.
Official rates declined to 6.25 percent at the end of 1996 from nine percent at the beginning of the year. They have since fallen another quarter point to 6.00 percent.

Telefonica de Espana, whose remaining 20.9 percent state stake is currently being privatised, has estimated receipts of 650 billion pesetas from the sale if the share price is 3,300 pesetas. Telefonica shares closed at 3,240 on Monday.

Both the deficit and debt are key criteria that Spain must adhere to this year to ensure its place at the launch of Europe's common currency scheduled for 1999. Other criteria cover inflation, exchange rates and long-term interest rates.

Under the terms agreed for the single currency, the deficit of each participating country must approach the reference value of three percent of GDP while debt must be at 60 percent of GDP or declining.
Folgado said although debt would be declining and the deficit to GDP would meet the reference value, financial markets would get little immediate mileage from the news.
The Spanish 10-year benchmark bond has already sharply outpaced its more solid German counterpart in recent months.
The spread between the yield, a measure of the added risk of holding Spanish debt, has narrowed sharply to 92 basis points on Monday from 330 basis points last Spring.
"The spread is going to be at an impasse in the first half," Folgado said "But from then it could fall through the spring of 1998.
The peseta, too, has been strong in recent weeks, although it has backed down from a recent run through resistance at 84.00. Late on Monday, it was trading at 84.12/15.
"I would prefer that the exchange rate hadn't appreciated so much. But the market rules," Folgado said. "We are near an equilibrium exchange rate." ($1=137.8 Peseta)
